contribution: The fourth unit of the French chapter: beginners introduce themselves at a research centre, say where they and others come from (de, d', du, des), ask simple questions about work, ask for help and follow directions on a building plan; the cultural part presents the CEA, the CNRS, the Cadarache centre with WEST, ITER as a separate international organisation next door, and the region around Saint-Paul-lez-Durance.
learn: introduce yourself at a research centre and say where you and other people come from.
ask for help politely and follow simple directions in a building.
explain what the CEA, the CNRS, Cadarache and ITER are and where they are in France.
prior: ITER and its seven members (chapter *ITER: why, where and who*)

activities.text: It is nine o'clock on the second day of your class's (imagined) visit. Your bus stops in front of a large modern building among oak trees and dry hills. Inside there is a reception desk, a long corridor, a lift and many doors. Your appointment is at ten, with a physicist whose name you have on a piece of paper. People with badges walk past you, speaking French, English and other languages.
activities.question: What will you say at the reception, and how will you find the right room?

activities.text:
Sentence starters

  • At the reception I need to say …
  • If I get lost, I can …
  • I think the researchers come from …, because …
  • A French research organisation I have heard of is …

activities.title: Think about it: a visit to a workplace
activities.prompt: What do you need to say when you arrive at a workplace you do not know: in Finland, and at an international research centre in France? Make a list. Then discuss: why would people from many countries work at the same place in Provence?
activities.pair: Discuss with a partner for three minutes, then write your list together.
activities.model: At the reception: greet, say our name, who we are (students from a Finnish school), who we have an appointment with and when. Later: ask where a room is, ask someone to repeat, thank. People from many countries work there because ITER is an international project: its members share the costs and the work, and they send their own engineers and scientists.
criteria: We list at least four things to say on arrival.
We include asking for help or for the way.
We give one reason why people from many countries work there.

activities.title: Warm-up: greeting and taking leave
activities.text: Revise the first lesson with a short video. Note the expressions you hear for greeting someone (*saluer*) and for leaving (*prendre congé*). Tick the ones you already know from *Bonjour ! Introducing yourself* and say one new one to your partner.

activities.title: Prediction 1: who runs Cadarache?
activities.prompt: The Cadarache research centre, next to ITER, is run by one French national organisation. Which one? Commit now; the theory summary will show you.

choices.text: the CEA, the atomic energy commission
choices.feedback: Right. Cadarache is one of the CEA's centres, where research began in 1959. The CNRS does fundamental research in every field; ITER is a separate international organisation next door.

choices.text: the CNRS, the national centre for science
choices.feedback: The CNRS is France's largest research organisation, but it does fundamental research in every field and does not run Cadarache. The centre belongs to the CEA, the atomic and alternative energy body.

choices.text: the ITER Organization, the global project
choices.feedback: ITER is built next to Cadarache, but it is a separate international organisation with seven members. Cadarache itself is a centre of the CEA, the French atomic and alternative energy body.

choices.text: EDF, the French electricity company
choices.feedback: EDF produces and sells electricity; it does not run research centres like Cadarache. Cadarache belongs to the CEA, the atomic and alternative energy body.

activities.title: Prediction 2: asking for help
activities.prompt: You are lost in a corridor and look for the library. A researcher you have never met walks past. What do you say first? Commit now; the theory summary will show you.

choices.text: Excusez-moi, madame. Je cherche la bibliothèque.
choices.feedback: Right: get her attention politely, then say what you need. Add s'il vous plaît and thank her: Merci beaucoup, c'est très gentil.

choices.text: Salut ! Elle est où, la bibliothèque ?
choices.feedback: The question is correct spoken French, but Salut is for friends. A researcher you have never met gets Excusez-moi, madame first.

choices.text: Où est la bibliothèque, s'il vous plaît ?
choices.feedback: Polite and understandable, but in French you first get the person's attention: Excusez-moi, madame. Je cherche la bibliothèque. Starting directly with the question can sound abrupt.

choices.text: Pardon, tu peux m'aider ? Je cherche la bibliothèque.
choices.feedback: Pardon is fine, but tu is for friends and people your age. To an adult you do not know at work: Excusez-moi, madame. Vous pouvez m'aider ?

activities.title: Listen: at a research centre
activities.text: Listen to each phrase, first slowly and then at normal speed, and repeat it aloud. The hints in italics use Finnish letters: capitals show the stressed syllable, *õ*, *ã* and *ẽ* are nasal vowels, *è* is an open *e*, *ž* is the *s* of English *pleasure* and *š* the Finnish *š*.

activities.title: At the reception
activities.text: Read the dialogue and notice three things: what Aino says about herself, how she checks that she understood the way, and how the conversation ends.

activities.title: Meeting a researcher
What did you notice?
activities.prompt: When Marc gives the way too fast, what does Aino do?

choices.text: She asks for it again, more slowly.
choices.feedback: Yes: Vous pouvez répéter plus lentement ? and then À gauche, puis tout droit. Repeating the way back is a simple way to check that you understood.

choices.text: She says she understands and leaves at once.
choices.feedback: Look again: she says Pardon, vous pouvez répéter plus lentement, s'il vous plaît ? and then repeats the way to check it.

choices.text: She switches to English and asks again.
choices.feedback: She stays in French: Vous pouvez répéter plus lentement ? Switching to English is fine when you are stuck, but here a slower repetition was enough.

choices.text: She asks another person in the corridor.
choices.feedback: She asks Marc himself to repeat more slowly, and then she repeats the way back to him to check: À gauche, puis tout droit.

sections: Science in France: CEA, CNRS and Cadarache
Asking for help and finding the way

activities.title: Back to your predictions
activities.prompt: Compare your two predictions with the theory. Then answer the opening question in English in one or two sentences: why do researchers from so many countries work in one quiet valley in Provence?

activities.title: Follow the directions
activities.text: Use the plan in the section *Asking for help and finding the way*.

activities.title: Where are you from?
Role-play: arriving at the research centre
activities.text:
Work in pairs with the plan of the building. **Round 1:** A takes card A, B takes card B. **Round 2:** swap: A takes card D, B takes card C. Read only your own card and do not show it. Speak without writing first; the word bank is a safety net.

Card A · Visitor

You are a Finnish student on a visit. Introduce yourself at the reception (name, school town, why you are here, your appointment at 14 h with Dr Rossi). Then ask how to find the library. Check that you understood, and thank.

Card B · Receptionist

Welcome the visitor, ask where he or she comes from, and give a badge. Dr Rossi is Italian and works on the first floor. Give the way to the library with the plan above. If the visitor asks you to repeat, repeat more slowly.

Card C · Visitor (swap)

You arrive late and you are lost. Stop a researcher in the corridor, explain who you are, and ask for help to find the conference room and the toilets. Ask one question about the researcher's work.

Card D · Researcher (swap)

Choose your country (Japan, India, Korea, the United States …) and your work (the magnets, the vacuum vessel, the computers). Answer the visitor's questions and give the way with the plan above.

Word bank

Bonjour, madame / monsieur, Je m'appelle …, Je suis lycéen / lycéenne, Je viens de / d' / du / des …, J'ai rendez-vous avec …, Excusez-moi, Je cherche …, Où est … ?, à gauche, à droite, tout droit, au bout du couloir, à côté de, en face de, au premier étage, Vous pouvez répéter plus lentement ?, Merci, c'est très gentil, Je vous en prie

Sentence starters

  • Bonjour, monsieur. Je m'appelle … J'ai rendez-vous avec …
  • Je suis lycéenne à …, en Finlande.
  • Excusez-moi, madame. Je cherche …
  • Qu'est-ce que vous faites ici ?
  • Vous venez d'où ?
  • À droite, puis au bout du couloir ? Merci beaucoup !

The receptionist or researcher: Je peux vous aider ?, Voici votre badge., C'est au premier étage., Je viens du Japon., Je travaille sur les aimants.

activities.title: Role-play: your dialogue
activities.prompt: After both rounds, write the French of round 1 or round 2, at least eight lines.
activities.pair: Perform the role-play with a partner first, then write it together. If you can, perform it for another pair, who follow the directions on the plan and check where you end up.
activities.model: **Round 1:** - B : Bonjour, monsieur. Je peux vous aider ? - A : Bonjour, madame. Je m'appelle Eetu Korhonen. J'ai rendez-vous avec le docteur Rossi à quatorze heures. - B : Vous venez d'où ? - A : Je viens de Finlande. Je suis lycéen à Espoo. Nous visitons ITER avec notre classe. - B : Bienvenue ! Voici votre badge. Le docteur Rossi travaille au premier étage. Prenez l'ascenseur, à droite. - A : Merci. Excusez-moi, je cherche aussi la bibliothèque. - B : C'est à gauche, en face des toilettes. - A : Pardon, vous pouvez répéter plus lentement ? - B : À gauche… en face des toilettes. - A : À gauche, en face des toilettes. Merci beaucoup, c'est très gentil ! - B : Je vous en prie. Bonne visite !
criteria: **Communicates the message:** we introduce ourselves (name, where we come from, why we are here) and ask for help or the way.
**Polite:** we use *vous*, *Excusez-moi*, *s'il vous plaît* and thank.
**Directions right:** the directions match the plan, and the listener can follow them.
**Checks understanding:** we ask for a repetition or repeat the way back at least once.

activities.title: Extension: a short cultural investigation
activities.text: Choose one: the CNRS, the CEA's centre at Saclay, the WEST tokamak, or the international school in Manosque. Find two facts about it on its own website or on Wikipédia (in French if you can: look for the numbers, the names and the words you recognise). Present them to another pair in English, with one French word you learned, and say where you found each fact and when it was written.

activities.title: 1. Where do they come from?
activities.prompt: Kenji, a researcher at ITER, comes from Japan. How does he say it?

choices.text: Je viens du Japon.
choices.feedback: Yes. Le Japon is masculine, so de + le becomes du.

choices.text: Je viens de Japon.
choices.feedback: De alone is for feminine countries like la Finlande. Le Japon is masculine: du Japon.

choices.text: Je viens des Japon.
choices.feedback: Des is for plural countries, like les États-Unis. Le Japon is masculine singular: du Japon.

choices.text: Je viens en Japon.
choices.feedback: En and au mean *in* or *to*, not *from*. *From* Japan is du Japon.

activities.title: 2. Which floor?
activities.prompt: The receptionist says: « Le laboratoire est au premier étage. » Where do you go?

choices.text: One floor up from the entrance level
choices.feedback: Yes. In France the entrance level is the rez-de-chaussée, and the premier étage is one floor up: in Finland, the *toinen kerros*.

choices.text: The floor of the entrance, the *1. kerros*
choices.feedback: In Finland the entrance level is the first floor, but in France it is the rez-de-chaussée. The premier étage is one floor up.

choices.text: The basement under the entrance
choices.feedback: The basement is the sous-sol. The premier étage is one floor above the entrance level.

choices.text: The top floor of the building
choices.feedback: Premier means *first*: the first floor above the rez-de-chaussée, one level up from the entrance.

activities.title: 3. ITER and Cadarache
activities.prompt: A friend says: *ITER and Cadarache are the same thing.* What is the best answer?

choices.text: No: ITER is a separate body next to it.
choices.feedback: Yes. Cadarache is a centre of the French CEA, with research since 1959. ITER is a separate international organisation with seven members, built next to it.

choices.text: Yes: Cadarache is the French name of ITER.
choices.feedback: Cadarache is the name of the place and of the CEA's research centre there. ITER is a separate international organisation built next to it.

choices.text: No: ITER is in Paris and Cadarache in Provence.
choices.feedback: Both are in Provence, in Saint-Paul-lez-Durance. Paris is where the ITER Agreement was signed in 2006. ITER is a separate international organisation next to the CEA's centre.

choices.text: ITER is a part of the CNRS at Cadarache.
choices.feedback: The CNRS does not run ITER or Cadarache. Cadarache belongs to the CEA, and ITER is a separate international organisation next to it.

activities.title: 4. Write: a message to the researcher
activities.prompt: Before the visit, write a short message in French (five or six sentences) to the researcher who will meet your class: greet, introduce yourself, say where you come from and why you are coming, ask one simple question about his or her work, and ask where you should meet. End politely.
activities.model: Bonjour, madame Sharma, Je m'appelle Aino Virtanen. Je suis lycéenne à Espoo, près d'Helsinki, en Finlande. Le 14 mai, nous visitons ITER avec notre classe de physique. Qu'est-ce que vous faites à ITER ? Où est-ce que nous vous retrouvons : à l'accueil ou au premier étage ? Merci beaucoup et à bientôt ! Aino
criteria: I greet politely and introduce myself (name, school, town, country).
I say why I am coming.
I ask one simple question with *vous* and ask where to meet.
I end politely (*Merci*, *À bientôt*).
